questions.q: What is a live SOC dashboard's primary job, according to this lesson?
options: To show what needs a human to act on right now, not to summarize history
To list every log source connected to the SIEM
To display the total number of alerts processed since the SIEM went live
To replace the need for any monthly or quarterly reporting
questions.explain: A dashboard looks at this second and points an analyst toward what needs attention next — that's different from a backward-looking report.

questions.q: Which three panels does this lesson identify as actually belonging on a live analyst dashboard?
options: Average employee headcount and the SOC's annual budget
A pie chart of every alert category since the SIEM went live
Lifetime log volume, a world map of source IPs, and total tickets ever closed
Open high-severity alerts, current queue depth, and systems under active investigation
questions.explain: Those three panels all answer the one question that matters mid-shift: what needs action right now?

questions.q: What is a "vanity metric" in the context of a SOC dashboard?
options: A number that is deliberately falsified to look better
A number that's accurate and often impressive but doesn't change what anyone does next
A metric that only appears in executive reports, never on analyst screens
Any metric that involves a percentage instead of a raw count
questions.explain: Lifetime log volume or total alerts processed are true numbers, but they don't drive any immediate decision — that's what makes them vanity metrics.

questions.q: How does dashboard clutter actually slow down triage, beyond just looking messy?
options: It has no real effect on response time, only on aesthetics
It causes the SIEM itself to process alerts more slowly
It only affects new analysts, never experienced ones
The time spent visually searching for the real signal adds directly onto detection time
questions.explain: Scanning a crowded screen for the panel that matters costs real seconds, and that search time adds to Mean Time to Detect.

questions.q: What happens when analysts learn that a dashboard is mostly noise?
options: They escalate every alert to Tier 2 regardless of severity
They immediately request the dashboard be deleted entirely
They stop trusting it and build their own workaround, so the dashboard fails silently
Nothing changes — analysts always use the official dashboard regardless
questions.explain: A dashboard that's quietly abandoned for a personal spreadsheet or saved search is worse than no dashboard, because leadership believes visibility exists when it doesn't.
